title: The Holy Spirit
hook: the Comforter, the one who comes alongside (John 14:26)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third day, anastasis, and the hinge the whole faith hangs on. Your line was death is not the end. What felt finished, and might not be? Day three hundred five.

Think of a courtroom. You're standing alone, accused of something, and you don't know the law. You don't know what to say. Your hands are shaking. Then the door opens, and someone walks in and stands right beside you. Not across the room. Beside you. They lean over and whisper: I'm here. I'll speak for you. I'll help you remember what to say. Now think of a hospital bed at night, and someone pulling up a chair next to it. Or a kid on the first day of school, and an older kid who sits down next to them at lunch. That movement, someone coming to stand beside you, is inside today's word. It's the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit on the night before he dies.
screen: `ALONE IN A COURTROOM.` → `SOMEONE STANDS BESIDE YOU.` → `THE NIGHT BEFORE HE DIES.`

segments.voice: Paraclete comes straight from the Greek parakletos. Para, beside, as in parallel. And kletos, called. One called to stand beside you. In a Greek courtroom, it was the word for a friend or advocate who spoke up for you. At the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, Jesus tells his frightened friends that he's leaving, but that they won't be left alone. "But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you." He also calls the Spirit "another Comforter." Another, because Jesus himself has been one. In First John, Jesus is called our advocate with the Father, the same Greek word. Translators have struggled with it for centuries. Advocate. Helper. Counselor. Comforter. The King James chose Comforter, and here's a thing worth knowing: in older English, comfort came from the Latin for with strength. To comfort someone was to strengthen them, not just to soothe them. So the Paraclete isn't only a warm blanket. It's a friend who stands beside you and makes you strong enough to stand. Christians say the Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, fully God, the one who hovered over the waters in Genesis, came like a dove at Jesus's baptism and like fire at Pentecost. Remember the filioque, from day two hundred eighty-six: East and West still differ on exactly how the Spirit proceeds. But all of them pray the same thing: that the Comforter comes.
screen: `PARA-KLETOS: CALLED TO YOUR SIDE.` · `ANOTHER COMFORTER.` · `COMFORT: WITH STRENGTH.` · `WATERS, DOVE, AND FIRE.` · then, large: `HE SHALL TEACH YOU ALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for comfort. Settle, and breathe. Think of where you feel alone right now, or where you need strength. Don't hurry past it. Then imagine someone coming to stand right beside you. Not fixing it. Just there, at your side, making you strong enough to stay. If you pray, you can ask the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, to come. If you don't, just let yourself be accompanied by that picture, and breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Paraclete. From the Greek, one called to your side: advocate, helper, comforter. Jesus's name for the Holy Spirit.
Your line: the comforter comes. Today, be a paraclete for someone: go and stand beside a person who's facing something alone. Day three hundred five.

howItsDone: Christians pray to the Holy Spirit especially at Pentecost, at baptisms and confirmations, and before reading scripture, often with old hymns such as "Come, Holy Ghost, our souls inspire."

original.note: Greek: one called to your side. An advocate or helper: John's word for the Holy Spirit.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Comforter means someone who makes you feel cozy.
what it means: the Holy Spirit as one who comes to stand beside you, speaks for you, and makes you strong.
what a scholar hears: parakletos, a legal advocate; used of the Spirit in John 14–16 and of Jesus in 1 John 2:1.

sources.quoted: But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.

notes: Etymology: parakletos from para + kalein (to call); 'kletos' is used here as a simplification of the verbal adjective. Confirm.
'Comfort' from Late Latin confortare, to strengthen (con + fortis). Confirm.
Wycliffe and Tyndale also used 'Comforter'; script credits the King James.
The howItsDone hymn line 'Come, Holy Ghost, our souls inspire' is John Cosin's 1627 translation of Veni Creator Spiritus (public domain). Confirm wording.
